title: How many gods?
hookLine: a sage at King Janaka's court is asked how many gods there are, and counts down from thousands to one

lines: A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.
cards: A king named Janaka pens up a thousand cows, with gold tied to their horns, and announces: these go to the wisest one here.
Nobody dares move, except a sage named Yajnavalkya, who calmly tells his student: drive them home. The court erupts. One by one, the learned stand up to test him.
Near the end comes Shakalya, and his question is one Hindu kids still get asked at lunch tables: how many gods are there?

teach.b: The story is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Yajnavalkya answers: three thousand three hundred and six. Shakalya says, yes, but how many, really?
Three. Two. One and a half.
And at last: one. Which is the one god? The breath, Yajnavalkya says.

It is Brahman, and they call it simply: that. Here's the teaching under the count. Hindus honor many gods, Ganesha, Lakshmi, Shiva, the goddess, and many Hindus understand them as faces of one reality, Brahman.

teach.h: EKAM SAT: ONE, CALLED BY MANY NAMES.
teach.b: An older line in the Rig Veda says it in a breath: ekam sat, the one that is, vipra bahudha vadanti, the sages call by many names. Not every Hindu reads that the same way.
Some worship one god, Vishnu or Shiva or the Devi, as supreme, and see the others as that god's forms or helpers. Others understand Brahman as beyond every form at all.
And next year, the schools of thought take the question one at a time.
They're called darshanas, and darshana means seeing, the same word as darshan at a temple, when you go to see the deity.
Each school is a way of seeing the one and the many, and their teachers argued, sometimes sharply.
So when a friend asks how many gods Hindus have, there's an old answer from Janaka's court: count as high as you like; Yajnavalkya came down to one.

how: Many Hindus explain their many gods with the Rig Veda's line ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti, and many families keep several deities side by side in one home shrine.

o: a way of seeing, the name for a school of thought
a temple bell rung to open the morning prayers
a ritual fire lit to open a temple festival

p: a way of seeing, a view
counted the gods down to one
the one reality behind the names

s: Hindus believe in millions of separate, competing gods
many Hindus see the many gods as faces of one reality; Yajnavalkya counted from 3,306 down to one.
Yajnavalkya's last answer was one god, Brahman
he called the one god the breath, Brahman, called simply 'that'.
every Hindu reads the one and the many the same way
some worship Vishnu, Shiva or the Devi as supreme; some hear Brahman beyond every form. the schools argue it out.

games.q: you're Yajnavalkya. Shakalya keeps pushing: but how many gods, really? what's your last answer?
o: none: the gods are only stories.
games.why: 3,306, then 33, 6, 3, 2, one and a half, one. the one is Brahman. the Rig Veda says it shorter: the one that is, the sages call by many names.

practice: Hindus have whole hymns that are nothing but names of God. Try three. Choose names your family uses, maybe Ram, Krishna, Ma, Shiva, and say one slowly with each breath out.
After each name, rest in the quiet that follows; notice it's the same quiet after every name.
If you pray, let the last name be the one closest to you; if you don't, say three things you love instead, and notice the one attention underneath them.

wordCard.voice: Darshana. A way of seeing: the word for each school of thought ahead, and the same word as darshan at a temple. Many ways of seeing, one reality seen.

orig.note: Sanskrit: darshana, seeing, a view. The word for the schools of thought, and the same word as darshan at a temple.

carryVoice: Your line: many names, one reality. Yajnavalkya counted down from thousands to one. I'll be here tomorrow.
